detailed_solution.concept: Engineering Mathematics - Linear Algebra
detailed_solution.markdown:
With the given order we can say that order of matrices are as follows:

$$\begin{aligned}   X^{T} &\rightarrow 3\times 4 \\     Y & \rightarrow 4\times 3 \\   X^{T}Y & \rightarrow 3\times 3 \\   \left ( X^{T}Y \right )^{-1} & \rightarrow 3\times 3 \\     P & \rightarrow 2\times 3 \\    P^{T} & \rightarrow 3\times 2 \\   P\left ( X^{T}Y \right )^{-1}P^{T} & \rightarrow \left ( 2\times 3 \right )\left ( 3\times 3 \right )\left ( 3\times 2 \right ) \\     & \rightarrow 2\times 2 \\ \therefore\;\; \left ( P\left ( X^{T}Y \right )^{-1}P^{T} \right )^{T} & \rightarrow 2\times 2 \end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the correct answer is **A**.

pp:ce:2005:q3.title: GATE CE 2005 | Set 1 | Question: 3
pp:ce:2005:q3.question: Which one of the following is NOT true for complex number $Z_1 \; and \; Z_2$?

detailed_solution.concept: Engineering Mathematics - Calculus
detailed_solution.markdown:
(A) is true since

$\frac{Z_{1}}{Z_{2}}=\frac{Z_{1}\bar{Z_{2}}}{Z_{2}\bar{Z_{2}}}=\frac{Z_{1}\bar{Z_{2}}}{\left | Z_{2} \right |^{2}}$

(B) is true by triangle inequality of complex number.

(C) is not true since $\left | Z_{1}-Z_{2} \right |\geq \left | Z_{1} \right |-\left | Z_{2} \right |$

(D) is true since

$$\begin{aligned}\left | Z_{1}+Z_{2} \right |^{2}&=\left ( Z_{1}+Z_{2} \right )\left ( \overline{Z_{1}+Z_{2}} \right ) \\   &=\left ( Z_{1}+Z_{2} \right )\left ( \bar{Z_{1}}+\bar{Z_{2}} \right ) \\   &=Z_{1}\bar{Z_{1}}+Z_{2}\bar{Z_{2}}+Z_{2}\bar{Z_{1}}+Z_{1}\bar{Z_{2}} \;\;...(i)\\ \left | Z_{1}-Z_{2} \right |^{2}&=\left ( Z_{1}+Z_{2} \right )\left ( \overline{Z_{1}-Z_{2}} \right ) \\   &=\left ( Z_{1}-Z_{2} \right )\left ( \bar{Z_{1}}-\bar{Z_{2}} \right ) \\   &=Z_{1}\bar{Z_{1}}+Z_{2}\bar{Z_{2}}-Z_{2}\bar{Z_{1}}-Z_{1}\bar{Z_{2}}\;\;...(ii)\end{aligned}$$

Adding (i) and (ii) we get,

$\left | Z_{1}+Z_{2} \right |^{2}+\left | Z_{1}-Z_{2} \right |^{2}=2Z_{1}\bar{Z_{2}}+2Z_{2}\bar{Z_{2}} =2\left | Z_{1} \right |^{2}+2\left | Z_{2} \right |^{2}$

Therefore, the correct answer is **C**.

pp:ce:2005:q9.title: GATE CE 2005 | Set 1 | Question: 9
pp:ce:2005:q9.question:
The components of strain tensor at a point in the plane strain case can be
obtained by measuring longitudinal strain in following directions

detailed_solution.concept: Solid Mechanics - Properties of Metals, Stress and Strain
detailed_solution.markdown:
In case of plane strain condition, the components

of strain tensor at a point are $\epsilon_{x}, \in_{y} \text{ and }\phi_{x y} .$

Here we have three unknowns so we require 3

equations to find them and these unknowns can

be find by the equations of longitudinal strain,

$\epsilon_{1}=\epsilon_{x} \cos ^{2} \theta_{1}+\epsilon_{y} \sin ^{2} \theta_{1}+\frac{\phi_{x y}}{2} \sin 2 \theta_{1}$

$\epsilon_{3}=\epsilon_{x} \cos ^{2} \theta_{3}+\epsilon_{y} \sin ^{2} \theta_{3}+\frac{\phi_{x y}}{2} \sin 2 \theta_{3}$

Therefore to find out component of strain tensor in

plain strain condition, we measure longitudinal

strains $\left(\epsilon_{1}, \epsilon_{2}\text{ and }\epsilon_{3}\right)$ along any three arbitrary direction.

Therefore, the correct answer is **B**.

detailed_solution.concept: Engineering Mathematics - Ordinary Differential Equation
detailed_solution.markdown:
Given,

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dt}+p\left ( t \right )y&=q\left ( t \right )y^{n};\, n\gt 0\\ \text{putting }  v&=y^{1-n} \\    \frac{dv}{dt}&=\left ( 1-n \right )y^{-n}\frac{dy}{dt} \\    \frac{dy}{dt}&=\frac{1}{\left ( 1-n \right )y^{-n}}\frac{dv}{dt}\end{aligned}$$

Substituting in the given differential equation, we get,

$\frac{1}{\left ( 1-n \right )y^{-n}}\frac{dy}{dt}+p\left ( t \right )y=q\left ( t \right )y^{n}$

Multiplying by $\left ( 1-n \right )y^{-n}$, we get,

$\frac{dv}{dt}+p\left ( t \right )\left ( 1-n \right )y^{1-n}=q\left ( t \right )\left ( 1-n \right )$

now since $y^{1-n}=v$, we get

$\frac{dv}{dt}+\left ( 1-n \right )pv=\left ( 1-n \right )q$

where p is p(t) and q is q(t).

Therefore, the correct answer is **A**.

pp:ce:2005:q34.title: GATE CE 2005 | Set 1 | Question: 34
pp:ce:2005:q34.question: The solution of $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}+2\frac{dy}{dx}+17y=0$; y(0)=1, $\frac{dy}{dx}(\frac{x}{4})=0$ in the range $0 \lt x \lt \frac{\pi}{4}$ is given by

detailed_solution.concept: Engineering Mathematics - Ordinary Differential Equation
detailed_solution.markdown:
$$\begin{aligned} \frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}+2\frac{dy}{dx}+17y&=0 \\     y\left ( 0 \right )&=1 \\    \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}\left ( \frac{\pi }{4} \right )&=0 \end{aligned}$$

This is a linear differential equation

$$\begin{aligned} D^{2}+2D+17&=0 \\   D&=-1\pm 4i \\ \therefore   \;\; y&=C_{1}e^{\left ( -1+4i \right )x}+C_{2}e^{\left ( -1-4i \right )x} \\    &=e^{-x}C_{1}e^{4xi}+C_{2}e^{-4xi} \\    &=e^{-x} \\ \left [ C_{1}\left ( \cos 4x+i\sin 4x \right ) \right ]& +C_{2}\left [ \cos \left ( 4x \right )+i\sin \left ( -4x \right ) \right ]\\ &=e^{-x}\left [ \left ( C_{1}+C_{2} \right )\cos 4x +\left ( C_{1}-C_{2} \right )i\sin 4x \right ] \\ \text{Let } C_{1}+C_{2}&=C_{3} \text{ and }\left ( C_{1}-C_{2} \right )i=C_{4} \\    y&=e^{-x}\left ( C_{3}\cos 4x+C_{4}\sin 4x \right )\\ \text{Since } y\left ( 0 \right )&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\;  1&=e^{-0}\left ( C_{3}\cos 0+C_{4}\sin 0 \right ) \\ \Rightarrow \;\;  C_{3}&=1 \\   \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}&=e^{-x}\left (-4C_{3}\sin 4x+4C_{4}\cos 4x \right ) \\ &-e^{-x}\left [ C_{3}\cos 4x+C_{4}\sin 4x \right ] \\    &=e^{-x}\left [ \left ( -4C_{3}-C_{4} \right )\sin 4x +\left ( 4C_{4}-C_{3}\cos 4x \right ) \right ] \\  \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x} \text{ at } x&=\frac{\pi }{4} \text{ is }0 \\ \therefore \; \left ( -4C_{4}-C_{3} \right )e^{-\pi /4}&=0 \\    4C_{4}&=C_{3} \\    C_{4}&=\frac{C_{3}}{4}=\frac{1}{4} \\ \therefore \;\;    C_{3}&=1 \text{ and }C_{4}=\frac{1}{4} \\    y&=e^{-x}\left ( \cos 4x+\frac{1}{4}\sin 4x \right ) \end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the correct answer is **A**.

pp:ce:2005:q35.title: GATE CE 2005 | Set 1 | Question: 35
pp:ce:2005:q35.question: Value of the integral $\oint_{c}(xydy-y^{2}dx)$, where c is the square cut from the first quadrant by the line x=1 and y=1 will be (Use Green's theorem to change the line integral into double integral)

detailed_solution.concept: Engineering Mathematics - Calculus
detailed_solution.markdown:
Green's theorem is,

$$\begin{aligned} \oint_{c} \phi dx + \Psi dy&=\int_{E}\left ( \frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial x}-\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial x} \right )\: dxdy\\ \text{Here }  I&=\oint_{c} \left ( xydy\: -\: y^{2}dx \right ) \\   &=\oint_{c} \left ( -y^{2} \right )dx\: +\: \left ( xy \right )dy \\ \therefore  \;\; \phi &=-y^{2},\; \Psi = xy \\    \frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial x}&=y,\; \frac{\partial \phi }{\partial y}=-2y\end{aligned}$$

Substituting in Green's Theorem, we get,

$$\begin{aligned}  I&= \int_{y=0}^{1}\int_{x=0}^{1}\left [ y-\left ( -2y \right ) \right ]dx\: dy \\   &= \int_{y=0}^{1}\int_{x=0}^{1}\: 3y\: dx\: dy \\   &= \int_{y=0}^{1}\left [ 3xy \right ]_{x=0}^{1}\: dy \\   &= \int_{y=0}^{1}3ydy=\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the correct answer is **C**.

To calculate $\frac{1}{a}$ using N-R method, set up the equation as,

$$\begin{aligned} x&=\frac{1}{a}\\    \frac{1}{x}&=a \\ \frac{1}{x_k}-a&=0\\  f\left ( x \right )&=\frac{1}{x_{k}}-a=0\\ \text{Now }  {f}'\left ( x \right )&=-\frac{1}{x^{2}} \\    f\left ( x_{k} \right )&=\frac{1}{x_{k}}-a \\    {f}'\left ( x_{k} \right )&=-\frac{1}{x^{2}_{k}}\\ &\text{For N-R method,}\\   x_{k+1}&=x_{k}-\frac{f\left ( x_{k} \right )}{{f}'\left ( x_{k} \right )} \\ \Rightarrow  \;\; x_{k+1}&=x_{k}-\frac{\left ( 1/x_{k}-a \right )}{-\frac{1}{x^{2}_{k}}} \end{aligned}$$

pp:ce:2005:q89.question:
A city is going to install the rapid sand filter after the sedimentation tanks. Use the following data.

Design loading rate to the filter : 200$m^{3}/m^2/d$
Design flow rate : 0.5$m^{3}/s$

The surface area required for the rapid sand filter will be

Therefore, the correct answer is **C**.
